title: Inquiry cites cocaine toxicity, delirium syndrome in death of Brooks man
subtitle: The Brooks, Alta., man who died after police fired a Taser at him in 2009 exhibited almost "super-human" strength while five police officers attempted to subdue him, a fatality inquiry concluded Wednesday. Five recommendations in the seven-page report focus on educating RCMP officers, dispatchers and emergency responders about a condition known as excited delirium syndrome, listed as one of two causes of death in the case of 40-year-old Grant William Prentice.
article: The Brooks, Alta., man who died after police fired a Taser at him in 2009 exhibited almost "super-human" strength while five police officers attempted to subdue him, a fatality inquiry concluded Wednesday.

Five recommendations in the seven-page report focus on educating RCMP officers, dispatchers and emergency responders about a condition known as excited delirium syndrome, listed as one of two causes of death in the case of 40-year-old Grant William Prentice.
Prentice died in hospital on May 6, 2009, from acute cocaine toxicity combined with excited delirium syndrome, after an altercation with police in which he was hit with a Taser once on each thigh.
The Taser wasn't effective in subduing Prentice, but he collapsed minutes later and then died in hospital.

According to the report, Prentice had ingested five times the level of cocaine that could be considered potentially fatal. Excited delirium syndrome has been observed to cause healthy young men who consumed cocaine to show extreme strength, incoherence, and high body temperature.
"They would, often after engaging in a physical fight, fall limp and shortly after die," the report states.

RCMP first responded to Lake Bevan Place in Brooks just after 7 p.m. that night for reports of a man attempting to enter a woman's house. According to the report, Prentice was staggering through the neighbourhood knocking on doors and ringing doorbells.
Resident Shannon Irving called police after Prentice tried to get into her home.
The report says Irving observed that Prentice had blood on his face and knee and looked pale and pasty with blotchy skin.

The two police officers who first attended the scene could not get Prentice to stop walking or talk to them, the report said. They took him to the ground but still were unable to subdue the 40-year-old, even after they fired the Taser at him.
Three more officers attended the scene and police were eventually able to handcuff Prentice.
About 10 or 15 minutes later, he went limp, the report said.
According to the report, Prentice was "unconscious, unresponsive, cyanotic and in obvious respiratory distress."
Prentice was then transported to hospital, where he later died.

In its recommendations, the report states that "in this particular set of circumstances, it is difficult to see that the attending emergency personnel, either the police officers or the EMS could have done anything different to prevent Mr. Prentice's death."
The report suggests early identification of the syndrome is important for saving the lives of potential patients.
"As individuals who present with this syndrome may suffer quick and fatal consequences, it is imperative that officers have an understanding as to identifying and dealing with it," the report states.
The report does not state how or if the Taser used by police played a role in Prentice's death.
Studies of excited delirium syndrome are in their infancy, but the term has shown up in previous fatality inquiries involving Taser-related deaths.

In 2011, the Alberta Serious Incident Response Team concluded that Gordon Walker Bowe died of excited delirium while high on cocaine, not as a result of the stun gun that was used against the men, who allegedly broke into a residence in Erin Woods three years earlier.
